title: the coronation planned
hook: the second book opens with an old king asking a hall full of people a question

segments.voice: Yesterday: Parashurama's challenge, answered. Rama strung the bow and spared the sage, who said, leave me my power to move, and the first book closed quietly at home. Did you let a win land softly? Today the second book opens: the Ayodhya Kanda. Day five hundred fourteen.

Many people know how the second book of the Ramayana ends: a prince in clothes made of bark, walking into the forest with his wife and his brother. So it's worth noticing how it begins. Not with a villain. Not with a quarrel. It begins with an old man who loves his son, and a room full of people who love him too. For the next few weeks, almost everything turns on one family's household, and the first thing in it is good news.
screen: `BARK CLOTHES AND A FOREST: THE END.` → `THE BEGINNING: GOOD NEWS.` → `ONE FAMILY'S HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha has ruled a long time, and he feels it. He loves all four of his sons, the text says, but Rama is the one the whole city talks about. Valmiki pauses to describe him, and one detail stands out. If someone does Rama a single kindness, he is pleased by it. If someone does him a hundred wrongs, he doesn't keep count. Generous memory is how Valmiki introduces the man about to lose everything. So the king makes a plan. He will name Rama the yuvaraja, the young king, the heir who shares the rule while his father is still alive. But he doesn't simply announce it. He calls an assembly: counselors, leading citizens, and kings from the lands around. The text notes, a little pointedly, that in his hurry he didn't send for Janaka, Sita's father, or for the king of Kekaya, Bharata's grandfather. Then Dasharatha speaks. I've carried this kingdom a long time, he says. My body is tired. I want to put the weight on my eldest son. If you agree, tell me. If there's a better course, tell me that too. The hall answers with one roar of yes. And the old king tests them. Why do you want Rama, he asks, while I'm still ruling well? So they tell him. They list Rama's truthfulness, his courage, his kindness to ordinary people, how he asks after their families and their fields when he comes back from a journey. The choice is public, and it's glad. That's why what happens next will hurt so much.
screen: `AN OLD KING, A LONG REIGN.` · `ONE KINDNESS KEPT, A HUNDRED WRONGS NOT.` · `THE KING ASKS THE ASSEMBLY.` · `WHY RAMA? THE PEOPLE ANSWER.` · then, large: `THE CHOICE IS PUBLIC, AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one kindness someone did for you this year, small or large. Let it be vivid: the place, the face, what they said. Hold it there. If a hurt from the same person or the same year tries to crowd in, notice it, and let it sit further back for now. Spend the rest of the sit with the kindness. The bell holds the time.
Yuvaraja, the young king who shares the rule while his father still reigns. Dasharatha proposes Rama for the title, and asks his assembly, which answers with joy.
Your line: he doesn't keep count. Today, keep count of one kindness and let one small wrong go uncounted. Day five hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Ayodhya Kanda as the heart of the Ramayana, and Rama's habit of remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs is often quoted as a model of character.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha, old and tired, ready to share the throne. how do you do it?
options: ask an assembly whether they agree.
fork.reveal: he asks the assembly, invites them to propose a better course, and even tests them: why Rama? they answer with his virtues.

original.note: Sanskrit yuvarāja: young king. the heir named while the father still reigns, the title Dasharatha means to give Rama.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama is about to become king.
what it means: he's to be made yuvaraja, heir and co-ruler, while his father still reigns.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki notes that Janaka and the king of Kekaya weren't sent for, a small detail that later readers have taken as a hint of the king's haste.
